name: Maple
tagline: Smooth, pale, and the painter's favorite.
short: Hard maple offers a creamy, almost uniform grain that takes paint and light stains beautifully. It is the workhorse of modern shaker and slab cabinetry across Brooklyn and Manhattan.
grain: Fine, closed, mostly straight with occasional curl
pros: Excellent paint finish: no grain bleed-through
cons: Can blotch under oil stains without prep
Yellows slightly with UV over time when clear-coated
Less dramatic grain than oak or walnut

name: American Walnut
tagline: Rich chocolate tones with quiet luxury.
short: Black walnut is the prestige hardwood of American cabinetmaking: deep brown heartwood, gentle figure, and a soft, hand-finished feel that elevates any kitchen, library, or vanity.
color: Deep chocolate brown with purple undertones
grain: Medium, mostly straight, occasional waves and burl
pros: Naturally rich color: no stain required
One of the most dimensionally stable hardwoods
Reads as luxury without dramatic figure
cons: Premium price tier (2-3× maple, 30-50% over white oak)
Sapwood-heartwood color contrast must be sorted carefully
Softer than maple or oak: more prone to denting
Lightens with UV exposure over decades

name: White Oak
tagline: The defining wood of modern American kitchens.
short: White oak combines visible cathedral grain, exceptional hardness, and a cool tan tone that takes everything from rift-cut natural finishes to Belgian-inspired smoked stains.
color: Light to medium tan with olive undertones
grain: Open-pored, prominent cathedral or straight rift
pros: Takes reactive, fumed, and pigment stains beautifully
On-trend for modern, transitional, and traditional kitchens
Most flexible aesthetic range of any hardwood
cons: Open grain shows under paint without filling
Rift-and-quartered cuts cost 30-100% more than plain-sawn
Tannins can react with metal fasteners and some finishes
Lead times longer than red oak or maple

name: Red Oak
short: Red oak's pinkish heartwood and pronounced cathedral grain defined American kitchens for half a century. Modern stains and rift cuts have brought it roaring back as a budget-friendly white oak alternative.
pros: Strong, hard, and easy to repair
Rift-cut version reads as modern Scandinavian
cons: Open grain is not watertight: avoid for wet zones
Pinkish undertone can clash with cool palettes
Less dimensionally stable than white oak
Wrong stain choice can read as dated builder-grade

name: Birch
short: Yellow birch offers maple-like density at a more accessible price. Its subtle grain finishes smooth under paint and takes a range of warm stains, making it the value pick for shaker and slab cabinetry.
color: Creamy white sap, light yellow-brown heart
grain: Fine, closed, mostly straight with subtle curl
pros: Maple-like density at a lower price
Best plywood substrate for cabinet construction
cons: Blotches under oil-based stains without prep
Yellows under UV exposure
Less dramatic grain than oak

name: Cherry
tagline: Patinas to a deep amber with age.
short: American black cherry begins as a soft pinkish blonde and matures over months into a glowing reddish-amber. It is the heritage hardwood of Shaker and Federal furniture, prized for its silky finish.
color: Pale pink-blonde aging to deep reddish amber
grain: Fine, closed, straight with occasional curl or pin knots
pros: Develops a unique amber patina over time
cons: Color shift can surprise clients (sample with patina)
Blotches under stains without conditioner
Softer than oak or maple: gentler use

name: Hickory
short: Hickory delivers the most dramatic color contrast and the highest Janka rating of any common cabinet wood. It is the right call for high-traffic kitchens, mountain houses, and rustic-modern aesthetics.
color: Cream sap with warm reddish-brown heart
grain: Bold, mostly straight, occasional wild figure
cons: Hard on tooling: premium pricing on labor
Strong color contrast not everyone wants
Less dimensionally stable than oak or walnut
Wrong choice for minimalist or modern aesthetics

name: White Ash
tagline: Oak-like grain, cleaner color, lower price.
short: White ash has the bold open grain of oak with a paler, more neutral background: perfect for clients who want oak texture without oak's pink or olive undertones. It also accepts cerused and limed finishes beautifully.
color: Pale neutral tan with light heartwood
grain: Open-pored, prominent cathedral, similar to oak
pros: Takes cerused and limed finishes cleanly
cons: Supply impacted by emerald ash borer
Open grain telegraphs under paint
Less recognizable to clients than oak

name: Mahogany
tagline: The original luxury hardwood, ribbon-figured and timeless.
short: True mahogany develops a deep reddish-brown patina, takes a piano-grade finish, and is dimensionally rock-solid. We specify African (Khaya) for sustainable sourcing while preserving the classic look.
pros: Takes high-gloss and hand-rubbed finishes beautifully
Develops a rich patina over decades
cons: Premium price tier
Sourcing requires care for sustainability
Softer than maple/oak: less ideal for high-traffic bases

name: Knotty Alder
tagline: Warm rustic character at a friendly price.
short: Knotty alder brings honest character knots, warm honey tones, and a soft hand-feel to rustic, mountain-modern, and Spanish revival kitchens. It is also the standard substrate for mid-priced stained cabinetry.
grain: Fine, mostly straight, with character knots when knotty grade
cons: Soft (Janka 590): dents easily
Knots can fall out if poorly sorted
Less suited to modern/minimalist looks

name: European Beech
tagline: Dense, pale, and the staple of European frameless cabinetry.
short: Steamed European beech offers maple-like density with a pinkish-cream tone and a uniform grain that has defined Bauhaus and Scandinavian cabinetry for nearly a century.
pros: Excellent paint and clear finish surface
cons: Less dimensionally stable than maple
Pinkish cast not loved by every palette
Lower availability in U.S. domestic supply

name: Rift-Cut White Oak
tagline: The defining cut of modern luxury kitchens.
short: Rift-cut white oak shows tight, ruler-straight vertical grain with no cathedral arches. It's the most consistent door-to-door look in cabinetry and the signature of post-2018 high-end design.
color: Light to medium tan with olive undertones
pros: Most consistent door-to-door grain match available
Reads as calm and modern: no cathedral noise
More dimensionally stable than plain-sawn (cuts perpendicular to rings)
Same hardness and water resistance as plain white oak
cons: 30-40% more expensive per board foot than plain-sawn
Lower yield = longer lead times for custom widths
Wastes the cut's beauty if you plan to paint it
Less character than plain-sawn for traditional kitchens

name: Quartersawn Oak
tagline: Iridescent ray fleck and the soul of Mission and Greene & Greene.
short: Quartersawn oak is sliced perpendicular to the growth rings, exposing the medullary rays as shimmering silver-gold ribbons. It is the defining wood of Arts & Crafts, Mission, and Stickley furniture.
color: Tan to medium brown with shimmering ray fleck
grain: Straight grain face with prominent medullary ray fleck
pros: Most dimensionally stable cut available: minimal seasonal movement
Iridescent ray fleck is impossible to replicate any other way
Defining wood of American Arts & Crafts and Mission style
Holds tight joinery in NYC's humidity swings
cons: Most expensive cut of oak: roughly 2× plain-sawn cost
Lowest yield per log = longest lead times (10-14 weeks)
Strong visual character can overwhelm minimalist designs
Ray fleck makes inconsistent panel matching harder to manage

name: Rustic Hickory
tagline: The hardest domestic hardwood: with knots, color swings, and farmhouse soul.
short: Rustic hickory is character-grade hickory selected for visible knots, mineral streaks, and dramatic heartwood-sapwood contrast. It is the signature wood of mountain modern, farmhouse, and lodge-style kitchens.
color: Dramatic creamy white sap to reddish-brown heart with knots
grain: Bold, open, often wavy, with mineral streaks and tight knots
pros: Hardest domestic cabinet wood: Janka 1,820 lbf
More affordable than clean-grade hickory (10-15% less)
Hides dents, scratches, and dings exceptionally well
cons: Strong visual character not for minimalist kitchens
Hard on tooling: slightly higher labor cost
Less dimensionally stable than oak or maple in humidity swings
Requires intentional color sorting to balance panels
